modules.name: Clock
modules.header:
Reading a clock, and waiting on one.
Which clock is being read matters more than the reading: `ClockMonotonic` counts forward from an arbitrary point
and never jumps, while `ClockRealtime` tracks wall time and can move in either direction when something sets it.
A duration is measured with the first; a timestamp anyone else will see is taken from the second.

modules.name: Dynamic
modules.header:
Loading a shared object at run time, and finding a symbol inside it.
This is the one part of the Linux interface that is not a system call. The kernel knows nothing about `dlopen`:
resolution, relocation and reference counting are all the dynamic linker's, and the entry points live in libc.
That is why this module links a library where the rest of the package links nothing.
The names are the platform's own, lowercase, because they are the symbols the loader exports and what a reader
porting code will look for.

modules.name: Entropy
modules.header:
Unpredictable bytes, from the kernel's own generator.
This is the only source in this package worth using for a key, a token, or anything an adversary would like to
guess. It draws from the same pool `/dev/urandom` exposes, without needing a descriptor — which matters, because
opening a file can fail in ways a security decision should not depend on.
The call can return fewer bytes than asked for, and a caller who needs all of them has to loop. That is not an
error condition: a request larger than 256 bytes may be cut short by a signal.

modules.name: Errors
modules.header:
How a Linux system call reports failure, and the numbers it reports.
There is no `errno` here. The kernel returns the error in the result register as a small negative number, and libc
is what turns that into a positive `errno` and a `-1` return. This package calls the kernel directly, so a caller
tests the raw result with `IsError` and reads the number with `Errno`.
The reserved range is `-4095` through `-1`. Nothing else is an error, which is what makes `mmap` workable: a
mapping address is an unsigned value that may legitimately have its top bit set, and only the last page of the
address space could collide with the error range, which the kernel never hands out.
The names keep the kernel's own spelling. `EINVAL` is what a man page names and what a reader porting code will
look for, and there is no Rux name for it that would be clearer. The values below are the architecture-independent
ones from `asm-generic/errno-base.h` and `asm-generic/errno.h`, which both supported architectures use.

modules.name: File
modules.header:
Reading and writing through a file descriptor, and the three descriptors a process starts with.
The wrappers here name their arguments and nothing more: each returns the kernel's raw result, which is a byte
count or a small negative error number. A short count is not an error and not an end of file — a read that returns
fewer bytes than asked for has to be called again, which is the caller's loop to write.

modules.name: Memory
modules.header:
Mapping and unmapping address space, and moving the program break.
These are the calls an allocator is built on. Nothing here tracks what it hands out: an address returned by `Mmap`
is valid until `Munmap` releases exactly the range that was mapped, and this package has no way to notice a caller
releasing a range it never mapped.

modules.name: Process
modules.header:
What a process can ask or say about itself.
Nothing here creates a process. `fork` and `execve` need signal handling, descriptor inheritance and a wait
protocol to be usable rather than merely callable, and a raw binding to them would be an invitation to get all
three wrong; that belongs above this package.

modules.name: Syscall
modules.header:
The raw system-call entry points, and the numbers that select a call.
This is the whole of what this package rests on: every wrapper elsewhere is one of these seven functions with the
arguments named. A caller may use them directly for a call this package does not wrap, which is what they are
public for — the numbering is the architecture's, so a number from one architecture means something else on the
other, and `SysRead` and its relatives are what keeps that straight.
A raw result is not yet an answer. It is either a value or a small negative error number, which `Errors::IsError`
and `Errors::Errno` are for.

modules.name: Types
modules.header:
The kernel ABI's own types: what a Linux system call takes and gives back.
These are the types the kernel interface is written in, not the ones libc presents. They are the same on both
supported architectures, because the kernel's 64-bit ABI fixes each width rather than letting the C data model
choose: `long` questions do not arise here the way they do in `Rux/C`.
A structure below is laid out as the kernel lays it out, and is passed by address to the call that fills it.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_REALTIME`: wall-clock time, which can jump when the system clock is set.
doc.markdown: `CLOCK_REALTIME`: wall-clock time, which can jump when the system clock is set.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`: time since an unspecified point, which never goes backwards.
doc.markdown:
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`: time since an unspecified point, which never goes backwards.
Not comparable between boots, and not the clock to record a timestamp with. It is the one to measure a duration
with, because setting the system clock cannot affect it.

items.name: ClockGetTime
items.signature: pub func ClockGetTime(clockId: int32, time: *var Timespec) -> int64

doc.summary: Reads `clockId` into `time`.
doc.markdown:
Reads `clockId` into `time`.
`clockId` is read by value; `time` is borrowed and written. Returns zero, or a negative error number — `EINVAL`
for a clock this kernel does not have.
`time` must be non-null and writable.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Nanosleep
items.signature: pub func Nanosleep(request: *Timespec, remaining: *var Timespec) -> int64

doc.summary: Suspends the caller for the requested duration.
doc.markdown:
Suspends the caller for the requested duration.
`request` is borrowed and read; `remaining` is borrowed and written when the wait was cut short, and may be null
when the caller does not care. Returns zero, or a negative error number.
A signal interrupts the wait and reports `EINTR` with the unslept time in `remaining`, which is what makes the
second argument worth passing: resuming means calling again with what came back, not with the original request.
The wait is against `ClockRealtime` but is not affected by the clock being set.
`request` must be non-null, and its nanoseconds must be under one second or the call reports `EINVAL`.

params.name: remaining
params.markdown: receives the unslept time when a signal cut the wait short, and may be null

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID`: processor time this process has used.
doc.markdown: `CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID`: processor time this process has used.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID`: processor time this thread has used.
doc.markdown: `CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID`: processor time this thread has used.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW`: like `ClockMonotonic`, but not adjusted by time synchronization.
doc.markdown:
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW`: like `ClockMonotonic`, but not adjusted by time synchronization.
Ticks at the hardware's own rate rather than a corrected one, which makes it the wrong clock for measuring a
duration anyone will compare against a wall clock, and the right one for measuring the hardware.

doc.summary: `TIMER_ABSTIME`: `ClockNanosleep` should treat its time as an absolute deadline.
doc.markdown: `TIMER_ABSTIME`: `ClockNanosleep` should treat its time as an absolute deadline.

items.name: ClockGetResolution
items.signature: pub func ClockGetResolution(clockId: int32, resolution: *var Timespec) -> int64

doc.summary: Reads the resolution of `clockId` into `resolution`.
doc.markdown:
Reads the resolution of `clockId` into `resolution`.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. The resolution is the granularity the clock advances by, which is not
the cost of reading it and not a promise about accuracy.
`resolution` must be non-null and writable.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: ClockNanosleep
items.signature: pub func ClockNanosleep(clockId: int32, flags: int32, request: *Timespec, remaining: *var Timespec) -> int64

doc.summary: Suspends the caller against a named clock, optionally until an absolute time.
doc.markdown:
Suspends the caller against a named clock, optionally until an absolute time.
`flags` is zero for a relative wait or `TimerAbsolute` for a deadline. `remaining` is written only for a relative
wait that a signal cut short, and may be null. Returns zero, or a positive error number — this one call reports
its error positively rather than negatively, which is the kernel's inconsistency and not this binding's.
An absolute wait is what a loop should use: a relative wait restarted after a signal drifts, because the time
spent handling the signal is not counted.
`request` must be non-null.

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero for a relative wait, or `TimerAbsolute` for a deadline

params.name: request
params.markdown: how long to wait, or when to wake

params.name: remaining
params.markdown: receives the unslept time for a relative wait, and may be null

doc.returns: zero, or a positive error number

doc.summary: `RTLD_LAZY`: resolve a function symbol the first time it is called rather than at load.
doc.markdown: `RTLD_LAZY`: resolve a function symbol the first time it is called rather than at load.

doc.summary: `RTLD_NOW`: resolve every symbol before `dlopen` returns, so a missing one is reported there.
doc.markdown: `RTLD_NOW`: resolve every symbol before `dlopen` returns, so a missing one is reported there.

doc.summary: `RTLD_GLOBAL`: make this object's symbols available to objects loaded afterwards.
doc.markdown: `RTLD_GLOBAL`: make this object's symbols available to objects loaded afterwards.

doc.summary: `RTLD_LOCAL`: keep this object's symbols to itself, which is the default.
doc.markdown: `RTLD_LOCAL`: keep this object's symbols to itself, which is the default.

doc.summary: `RTLD_NODELETE`: do not unload the object when its last reference goes, so its storage stays valid.
doc.markdown: `RTLD_NODELETE`: do not unload the object when its last reference goes, so its storage stays valid.

doc.summary: `GRND_NONBLOCK`: report `EAGAIN` rather than waiting for the pool to be seeded.
doc.markdown: `GRND_NONBLOCK`: report `EAGAIN` rather than waiting for the pool to be seeded.

doc.summary: `GRND_RANDOM`: draw from the blocking pool, which is almost never what a caller wants.
doc.markdown:
`GRND_RANDOM`: draw from the blocking pool, which is almost never what a caller wants.
Kept for completeness. The default source is as unpredictable and does not stall.

items.name: GetRandom
items.signature: pub func GetRandom(buffer: *var opaque, length: uint, flags: uint32) -> int64

doc.summary: Fills up to `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
doc.markdown:
Fills up to `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
`buffer` is borrowed and written; `length` and `flags` are read by value. Returns the number of bytes actually
written, or a negative error number.
A short count is ordinary rather than a failure: a request over 256 bytes can be cut short by a signal, and a
caller needing the whole buffer must call again for the rest. Without `RandomNonBlocking` the first call in the
life of a system may wait for the pool to be seeded; after that it does not wait at all.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes. Treat a short count as bytes obtained, not as failure, or the
unwritten tail stays whatever it held — which for a key is the worst possible outcome.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes to ask for

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero, or one of the `Random*` values

doc.returns: the bytes written, which may be fewer than asked for, or a negative error number

Whether a raw system-call result is one of the kernel's reserved error values.

mapping address a memory call returns.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

`result` is read by value; the number is returned by copy, positive, as a man page names it. A successful result
gives zero, which is not an error number and never collides with one.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

items.name: Read
items.signature: pub func Read(fd: FileDescriptor, buffer: *var opaque, count: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Reads up to `count` bytes from `fd` into `buffer`.
doc.markdown:
Reads up to `count` bytes from `fd` into `buffer`.
`fd` and `count` are read by value; `buffer` is borrowed and written. Returns the number of bytes actually read,
zero at end of file, or a negative error number.
A count smaller than `count` is ordinary and is not an end of file: a pipe, a terminal, or a signal can each cut a
read short. Only zero means the source has ended.
`buffer` must be writable for `count` bytes. The kernel checks the address and reports `EFAULT` rather than
faulting, but it does not check the length against anything the caller knows.

params.name: count
params.markdown: how many bytes to ask for

doc.returns: the bytes read, zero at end of file, or a negative error number

items.name: Write
items.signature: pub func Write(fd: FileDescriptor, buffer: *opaque, count: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Writes up to `count` bytes from `buffer` to `fd`.
doc.markdown:
Writes up to `count` bytes from `buffer` to `fd`.
`fd` and `count` are read by value; `buffer` is borrowed and read. Returns the number of bytes actually written,
or a negative error number.
A count smaller than `count` is ordinary, and the rest has to be written by calling again from where this
stopped. Writing to a pipe whose reader has closed raises `SIGPIPE` before this can report `EPIPE`.
`buffer` must be readable for `count` bytes.
doc.returns: the bytes written, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Closes `fd` and releases what the kernel held for it.
doc.markdown:
Closes `fd` and releases what the kernel held for it.
`fd` is read by value. Returns zero, or a negative error number.
A failure does not mean the descriptor is still open: on Linux it is released whatever this reports, so retrying
a failed close can close a descriptor another thread has since opened under the same number.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `AT_FDCWD`: resolve a relative path against the current directory rather than a descriptor.
doc.markdown:
`AT_FDCWD`: resolve a relative path against the current directory rather than a descriptor.
The value every `*at` call takes when the caller means an ordinary path. It is `-100` rather than `-1` so that a
stray `-1` from a failed open cannot be mistaken for it.

doc.summary: `O_RDONLY`: open for reading only.
doc.markdown: `O_RDONLY`: open for reading only.

doc.summary: `O_WRONLY`: open for writing only.
doc.markdown: `O_WRONLY`: open for writing only.

doc.summary: `O_RDWR`: open for both reading and writing.
doc.markdown: `O_RDWR`: open for both reading and writing.

doc.summary: `O_CREAT`: create the file when it does not exist, which is when the mode argument is read.
doc.markdown: `O_CREAT`: create the file when it does not exist, which is when the mode argument is read.

doc.summary: `O_EXCL`: with `OpenCreate`, fail rather than open a file that already exists.
doc.markdown:
`O_EXCL`: with `OpenCreate`, fail rather than open a file that already exists.
The pair is what makes creating a file an atomic claim on the name.

doc.summary: `O_TRUNC`: truncate the file to nothing when opening it for writing.
doc.markdown: `O_TRUNC`: truncate the file to nothing when opening it for writing.

doc.summary: `O_APPEND`: every write goes to the end, atomically with respect to other appenders.
doc.markdown: `O_APPEND`: every write goes to the end, atomically with respect to other appenders.

doc.summary: `O_NONBLOCK`: reads and writes report `EAGAIN` rather than waiting.
doc.markdown: `O_NONBLOCK`: reads and writes report `EAGAIN` rather than waiting.

doc.summary: `O_CLOEXEC`: close this descriptor automatically when the process executes a new program.
doc.markdown:
`O_CLOEXEC`: close this descriptor automatically when the process executes a new program.
Worth setting on nearly everything: without it a descriptor leaks into every child, which is both a resource and
a confidentiality problem.

doc.summary: `O_DIRECTORY`: fail unless the target is a directory.
doc.markdown:
`O_DIRECTORY`: fail unless the target is a directory.
x86-64 kept the number it had before the generic table was drawn up. On AArch64 this same bit means
`O_DIRECT` instead, so a directory opened with the wrong number fails with `EINVAL` rather than opening.

doc.summary: `O_DIRECTORY`: fail unless the target is a directory.
doc.markdown:
`O_DIRECTORY`: fail unless the target is a directory.
AArch64 uses the generic table's number. x86-64 uses a different one, and its bit means `O_DIRECT` here,
so a directory opened with the wrong number fails with `EINVAL` rather than opening.

doc.summary: `SEEK_SET`: measure the new offset from the start of the file.
doc.markdown: `SEEK_SET`: measure the new offset from the start of the file.

doc.summary: `SEEK_CUR`: measure the new offset from the current one.
doc.markdown: `SEEK_CUR`: measure the new offset from the current one.

doc.summary: `SEEK_END`: measure the new offset from the end of the file.
doc.markdown: `SEEK_END`: measure the new offset from the end of the file.

items.name: OpenAt
items.signature: pub func OpenAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, flags: int32, mode: FileMode) -> int64

doc.summary: Opens `path` relative to `directoryFd` and returns a descriptor, or a negative error number.
doc.markdown:
Opens `path` relative to `directoryFd` and returns a descriptor, or a negative error number.
`directoryFd` is a descriptor for the directory a relative path is resolved against, or `AtFdCwd` for the current
one; an absolute path ignores it. `path` is borrowed and must be null-terminated. `flags` is one of the three
access modes combined with whatever else applies. `mode` is the permission bits a newly created file gets, and is
read only when `OpenCreate` is set.
This is the only open the package offers, because it is the only one AArch64 has.
`path` must be non-null and terminated. The mode is masked by the process umask, which this cannot see.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

params.name: path
params.markdown: the path to open, as a null-terminated byte string

params.name: flags
params.markdown: the access mode and the open flags, combined with `|`

params.name: mode
params.markdown: the permission bits for a file this creates, ignored otherwise

doc.returns: the new descriptor, or a negative error number

items.name: Lseek
items.signature: pub func Lseek(fd: FileDescriptor, offset: FileOffset, whence: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Moves the file offset of `fd` and returns where it ended up, or a negative error number.
doc.markdown:
Moves the file offset of `fd` and returns where it ended up, or a negative error number.
`offset` is measured from whichever origin `whence` names. Returns the resulting absolute offset.
Seeking past the end is allowed and creates a hole when something is later written there. A pipe or socket has no
offset to move and reports `ESPIPE`.

params.name: offset
params.markdown: how far to move, interpreted according to `whence`

doc.returns: the resulting offset from the start, or a negative error number

items.name: Getdents64
items.signature: pub func Getdents64(fd: FileDescriptor, buffer: *var opaque, count: uint) -> int64

doc.summary:
Reads directory entries from `fd` into `buffer`, and returns the bytes filled, zero at the end, or a negative
error number.
doc.markdown:
Reads directory entries from `fd` into `buffer`, and returns the bytes filled, zero at the end, or a negative
error number.
The buffer holds packed `linux_dirent64` records: inode at offset 0 (8 bytes), a seek cookie at 8 (8 bytes),
the record's length at 16 (2 bytes), the entry type at 18 (1 byte), and the NUL-terminated name from 19. The
kernel writes as many whole records as fit; call again for the rest.
doc.returns: the bytes filled, zero at the end of the directory, or a negative error number

items.name: LinkAt
items.signature: pub func LinkAt(oldDirectoryFd: FileDescriptor, oldPath: *char8, newDirectoryFd: FileDescriptor, newPath: *char8, flags: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Creates a hard link: `newPath` becomes a second name for the file `oldPath` names.
doc.markdown:
Creates a hard link: `newPath` becomes a second name for the file `oldPath` names.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. `flags` is zero to leave a symbolic link at `oldPath` unfollowed,
or `FollowSymlinks` to link what it points at.

params.name: newPath
params.markdown: the new name for the same file

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero, or `FollowSymlinks` to link what a final link points at

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `AT_SYMLINK_FOLLOW`: make `LinkAt` link a symbolic link's target rather than the link.
doc.markdown: `AT_SYMLINK_FOLLOW`: make `LinkAt` link a symbolic link's target rather than the link.

items.name: SymlinkAt
items.signature: pub func SymlinkAt(target: *char8, newDirectoryFd: FileDescriptor, linkPath: *char8) -> int64

doc.summary: Creates a symbolic link at `linkPath` holding `target` as its text.
doc.markdown:
Creates a symbolic link at `linkPath` holding `target` as its text.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. The target is stored, not checked: a dangling link is created as
readily as a good one, which is a property callers rely on.

params.name: target
params.markdown: the text the link will hold, which need not exist

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW`: act on a symbolic link itself rather than on what it points at.
doc.markdown: `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW`: act on a symbolic link itself rather than on what it points at.

items.name: FstatAt
items.signature: pub func FstatAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, statBuffer: *var opaque, flags: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Fills `statBuffer` with what the kernel knows about the file `path` names.
doc.markdown:
Fills `statBuffer` with what the kernel knows about the file `path` names.
The kernel's own name for this call is `newfstatat`, which `SysNewFstatAt` keeps; the wrapper is spelled the way
macOS and FreeBSD spell theirs, so one name reaches the call on all three systems.
`statBuffer` must be writable for the whole of the architecture's `struct stat`, whose layout this package
does not model: 144 bytes on x86-64 and 128 on AArch64, with the fields at different offsets in each.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero to follow a symbolic link at the end of the path, or `SymlinkNoFollow` to describe the link

params.name: path
params.markdown: the path to describe, as a null-terminated byte string

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: FchmodAt
items.signature: pub func FchmodAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, mode: FileMode, flags: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Sets the permission bits of the file `path` names.
doc.markdown:
Sets the permission bits of the file `path` names.
`directoryFd` is `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path. Returns zero, or a negative error number. Linux does not
support `SymlinkNoFollow` here and reports `EOPNOTSUPP` for it: a symbolic link's own bits mean nothing.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

params.name: path
params.markdown: the path whose bits are set

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero, or `SymlinkNoFollow` where the system supports it

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: UtimensAt
items.signature: pub func UtimensAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, times: *opaque, flags: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Sets the access and modification times of the file `path` names.
doc.markdown:
Sets the access and modification times of the file `path` names.
`times` is borrowed and holds two `timespec` values — access first, then modification — each a whole-second
count and a nanosecond fraction, both 8 bytes. A null `times` sets both to now. `flags` may carry
`SymlinkNoFollow`. Returns zero, or a negative error number.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

params.name: path
params.markdown: the path whose times are set

params.name: times
params.markdown: two `timespec` values, or null for now

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero to follow a final symbolic link, or `SymlinkNoFollow`

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Getcwd
items.signature: pub func Getcwd(buffer: *var char8, size: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Writes the current working directory's absolute path into `buffer`, NUL-terminated.
doc.markdown:
Writes the current working directory's absolute path into `buffer`, NUL-terminated.
Returns the length written including the terminator, or a negative error number; `ERANGE` where the buffer is
too small for the answer.
`buffer` must be writable for `size` bytes.

params.name: buffer
params.markdown: receives the working directory as a null-terminated path

doc.returns: the bytes written including the terminator, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Makes `path` the process's working directory.
doc.markdown:
Makes `path` the process's working directory.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. The change is process-wide and immediately visible to every thread,
which is why nothing above this should call it casually.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: ReadlinkAt
items.signature: pub func ReadlinkAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, buffer: *var char8, size: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Reads the text a symbolic link holds into `buffer`.
doc.markdown:
Reads the text a symbolic link holds into `buffer`.
`directoryFd` is `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path. Returns the number of bytes written, or a negative error
number. The text is **not** NUL-terminated, and is silently truncated where it does not fit, so a caller that
filled the buffer exactly cannot tell truncation from a perfect fit and should retry with more room.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

params.name: buffer
params.markdown: receives the link's text, without a terminator

doc.returns: the bytes written, which equals `size` when the text was truncated, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Flushes everything written to `fd` through to the storage device.
doc.markdown:
Flushes everything written to `fd` through to the storage device.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. Returning only once the device has acknowledged the write is the whole
point: without it, data a successful `Write` reported may still be lost to a power failure.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Ftruncate
items.signature: pub func Ftruncate(fd: FileDescriptor, length: FileOffset) -> int64

doc.summary: Sets the length of the file behind `fd` to `length`.
doc.markdown:
Sets the length of the file behind `fd` to `length`.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. Growing a file this way creates a hole rather than allocating, so a
later write into it can still fail with `ENOSPC`. Shrinking discards what was past the new end.

params.name: length
params.markdown: the size the file should have afterwards

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: UnlinkAt
items.signature: pub func UnlinkAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, flags: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Removes the name `path` from its directory.
doc.markdown:
Removes the name `path` from its directory.
`flags` is zero to remove a file, or `RemoveDirectory` to remove an empty directory. Returns zero, or a negative
error number.
Removing a name does not free the file: anything still holding it open keeps reading and writing it, and the
storage goes only when the last descriptor closes.
`path` must be non-null and terminated.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero for a file, or `RemoveDirectory` for a directory

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `AT_REMOVEDIR`: make `UnlinkAt` remove a directory rather than a file.
doc.markdown: `AT_REMOVEDIR`: make `UnlinkAt` remove a directory rather than a file.

items.name: MkdirAt
items.signature: pub func MkdirAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, mode: FileMode) -> int64

doc.summary: Creates a directory named `path` with permission bits `mode`.
doc.markdown:
Creates a directory named `path` with permission bits `mode`.
Returns zero, or a negative error number — `EEXIST` when the name is taken, which is how this is used as a lock.
`path` must be non-null and terminated. The mode is masked by the process umask.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: RenameAt
items.signature: pub func RenameAt(oldDirectoryFd: FileDescriptor, oldPath: *char8, newDirectoryFd: FileDescriptor, newPath: *char8) -> int64

doc.summary: Renames `oldPath` to `newPath`, each resolved against its own directory descriptor.
doc.markdown:
Renames `oldPath` to `newPath`, each resolved against its own directory descriptor.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. Within one file system this replaces any existing `newPath` atomically,
which is what makes it the way to publish a file that was written under a temporary name. Across file systems it
reports `EXDEV` rather than copying.
Both paths must be non-null and terminated.

params.name: newPath
params.markdown: the name to move it to

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Fstat
items.signature: pub func Fstat(fd: FileDescriptor, statBuffer: *var opaque) -> int64

doc.summary: Fills `statBuffer` with what the kernel knows about the file behind `fd`.
doc.markdown:
Fills `statBuffer` with what the kernel knows about the file behind `fd`.
`statBuffer` is borrowed and written with the kernel's `struct stat`, whose layout this package does not model:
it differs by architecture, and reading it needs a declaration that says which. Returns zero, or a negative error
number.
`statBuffer` must be writable for the whole of the architecture's `struct stat`, which is 144 bytes on x86-64 and
128 on AArch64. Nothing here checks that.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Dup3
items.signature: pub func Dup3(oldFd: FileDescriptor, newFd: FileDescriptor, flags: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Makes `newFd` a copy of `oldFd`, closing whatever `newFd` was.
doc.markdown:
Makes `newFd` a copy of `oldFd`, closing whatever `newFd` was.
`flags` may carry `OpenCloseOnExec`, which is the reason this exists rather than `dup2`: setting it afterwards
leaves a window in which another thread can execute a new program and leak the descriptor. Returns `newFd`, or a
negative error number.
Duplicating a descriptor onto itself reports `EINVAL` here, where `dup2` returned it unchanged.

params.name: newFd
params.markdown: the number the duplicate should have

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero, or `OpenCloseOnExec` for the new descriptor

doc.returns: `newFd`, or a negative error number

items.name: Pipe2
items.signature: pub func Pipe2(descriptors: *var int32, flags: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Creates a pipe and writes its two descriptors into `descriptors`.
doc.markdown:
Creates a pipe and writes its two descriptors into `descriptors`.
`descriptors` is borrowed and receives the reading end at index zero and the writing end at index one. `flags`
may carry `OpenCloseOnExec` and `OpenNonBlocking`. Returns zero, or a negative error number.
`descriptors` must be writable for two `int32` values.

params.name: descriptors
params.markdown: receives the read end at index zero and the write end at index one

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `PROT_NONE`: the pages may not be touched at all.
doc.markdown: `PROT_NONE`: the pages may not be touched at all.

doc.summary: `PROT_READ`: the pages may be read.
doc.markdown: `PROT_READ`: the pages may be read.

doc.summary: `PROT_WRITE`: the pages may be written.
doc.markdown: `PROT_WRITE`: the pages may be written.

doc.summary: `PROT_EXEC`: the pages may be executed.
doc.markdown: `PROT_EXEC`: the pages may be executed.

doc.summary: `MAP_SHARED`: writes are visible to other mappings of the same object and reach it.
doc.markdown: `MAP_SHARED`: writes are visible to other mappings of the same object and reach it.

doc.summary: `MAP_PRIVATE`: writes are private to this mapping and never reach the object.
doc.markdown: `MAP_PRIVATE`: writes are private to this mapping and never reach the object.

doc.summary: `MAP_FIXED`: place the mapping exactly at the requested address, replacing whatever was there.
doc.markdown:
`MAP_FIXED`: place the mapping exactly at the requested address, replacing whatever was there.
Dangerous by design: it silently unmaps anything already at the address, which may be someone else's mapping.

doc.summary: `MAP_ANONYMOUS`: the mapping is backed by zeroed pages rather than by a file.
doc.markdown:
`MAP_ANONYMOUS`: the mapping is backed by zeroed pages rather than by a file.
The descriptor argument is then unused and is conventionally `-1`.

items.name: Mmap
items.signature: pub func Mmap(address: *opaque, length: uint, protection: int32, flags: int32, fd: int32, offset: uint64) -> int64

doc.summary: Creates a mapping and returns its address, or a negative error number.
doc.markdown:
Creates a mapping and returns its address, or a negative error number.
`address` is a hint unless `MapFixed` is set, and null asks the kernel to choose. `length` is rounded up to a
whole number of pages. `fd` is the object to map, or `-1` with `MapAnonymous`. `offset` must be page-aligned.
Returns the mapping's address as an integer. Testing it needs `Errors::IsError` rather than a sign test: a valid
address may have its top bit set, and only the kernel's reserved `-4095` through `-1` range is a failure.
The mapping outlives nothing on its own — it stays until `Munmap` releases it or the process ends.
`MapFixed` replaces whatever occupies the address, including a mapping this program depends on.

params.name: address
params.markdown: a hint for where to map, or null to let the kernel choose

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes, rounded up to whole pages

params.name: protection
params.markdown: what may be done with the pages, as `Protection*` flags

params.name: fd
params.markdown: the file to map, or -1 with `MapAnonymous`

params.name: offset
params.markdown: where in the file the mapping starts

doc.returns: the mapping's address, or a negative error number

items.name: Munmap
items.signature: pub func Munmap(address: *opaque, length: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Releases the mapping that begins at `address` and spans `length` bytes.
doc.markdown:
Releases the mapping that begins at `address` and spans `length` bytes.
`address` must be page-aligned; `length` is rounded up to whole pages. Returns zero, or a negative error number.
Releasing a range that was never mapped succeeds and does nothing, so this cannot be used to discover whether a
range was mapped.
Every pointer into the range becomes invalid, and the address space may be handed to a later mapping at once.

params.name: address
params.markdown: a page-aligned address to release from

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Sets the program break and returns where it ended up.
doc.markdown:
Sets the program break and returns where it ended up.
`address` is the requested new break, or null to ask where it is. Returns the resulting break, which is the old
one when the request could not be met — this call reports failure by not moving rather than by an error number.
The break is a single process-wide value. Anything else in the process that uses it, including a C runtime that
was linked in, is using the same one.

params.name: address
params.markdown: where to move the program break, or null to read it

doc.returns: the resulting break, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `MADV_DONTNEED`: the pages are not needed, and the kernel may discard them.
doc.markdown:
`MADV_DONTNEED`: the pages are not needed, and the kernel may discard them.
An anonymous page discarded this way reads back as zero next time, which is how a range is released without
giving up the address space.

doc.summary: `MADV_WILLNEED`: the pages will be read soon, so reading them ahead is worthwhile.
doc.markdown: `MADV_WILLNEED`: the pages will be read soon, so reading them ahead is worthwhile.

doc.summary: `MADV_RANDOM`: the pages will be touched in no useful order, so reading ahead is not.
doc.markdown: `MADV_RANDOM`: the pages will be touched in no useful order, so reading ahead is not.

doc.summary: `MADV_SEQUENTIAL`: the pages will be touched in order.
doc.markdown: `MADV_SEQUENTIAL`: the pages will be touched in order.

items.name: Mprotect
items.signature: pub func Mprotect(address: *opaque, length: uint, protection: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Changes what may be done with the pages covering `address` through `address + length`.
doc.markdown:
Changes what may be done with the pages covering `address` through `address + length`.
`address` must be page-aligned; `length` is rounded up to whole pages. `protection` is the same set `Mmap` takes.
Returns zero, or a negative error number.
Removing a permission takes effect at once, so a thread touching the range concurrently faults rather than
finishing what it started.
Nothing here checks that the range was ever mapped, and marking executable memory writable at the same time is
what a hardened system refuses.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes, rounded up to whole pages

params.name: protection
params.markdown: what may be done with them afterwards

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Madvise
items.signature: pub func Madvise(address: *opaque, length: uint, advice: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Tells the kernel how the pages covering a range are about to be used.
doc.markdown:
Tells the kernel how the pages covering a range are about to be used.
`address` must be page-aligned. Returns zero, or a negative error number. Advice is advice: the kernel is free to
ignore all of it, with the exception of `AdviseDontNeed`, which actually discards.
`AdviseDontNeed` loses whatever the range held. On anonymous memory that is a zeroing; on a private file mapping
it discards the modifications rather than writing them back.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes the advice covers

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `AT_PAGESZ`: the auxiliary-vector entry holding the page size, in bytes.
doc.markdown: `AT_PAGESZ`: the auxiliary-vector entry holding the page size, in bytes.

doc.summary: `AT_NULL`: the entry that ends the auxiliary vector.
doc.markdown: `AT_NULL`: the entry that ends the auxiliary vector.

doc.summary: The size of a page, read out of this process's auxiliary vector.
doc.markdown:
The size of a page, read out of this process's auxiliary vector.
Linux publishes the page size in the auxiliary vector the kernel hands to a new process, not behind a system
call. libc captures that vector at startup and answers from it, which is what `getauxval` reads; this package
calls no libc and captures nothing at startup, so it asks the kernel for the same vector through the interface
that exposes it as a file, `/proc/self/auxv`. The file is a sequence of `(type, value)` pairs of unsigned
64-bit words, ending at a type of `AuxNull`.
The cost is an open, a read and a close, so a caller needing the size more than once should keep it rather than
ask again.
Reports the open's or the read's own error number when `/proc` is not mounted or not readable, which is
ordinary in a container built without it. Reports `-ENOENT` when the vector was readable but held no
`AuxPageSize` entry, and `-EINVAL` when it held one that is not a size the address space could have.
doc.returns: the page size in bytes, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Ends the calling thread's process with `code`.
doc.markdown:
Ends the calling thread's process with `code`.
`code` is read by value; only its low eight bits reach a waiting parent, which is the kernel's rule rather than
this binding's. Does not return.
Nothing is flushed, unwound, or destroyed on the way out: the kernel reclaims the address space and the
descriptors, and anything the program was holding elsewhere is simply gone.
This ends the whole process rather than one thread, which is `exit_group` in kernel terms.

params.name: code
params.markdown: the status to report to the parent

doc.summary: The calling process's own identifier.
doc.markdown:
The calling process's own identifier.
Takes nothing and returns the identifier by copy. Cannot fail: every process has one, and the call has no way to
be given a bad argument.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the calling process's identifier

doc.summary: `mmap(2)`'s system-call number.
doc.markdown: `mmap(2)`'s system-call number.

doc.summary: `getpid(2)`'s system-call number.
doc.markdown: `getpid(2)`'s system-call number.

doc.summary: `mmap(2)`'s system-call number.
doc.markdown: `mmap(2)`'s system-call number.

doc.summary: `getpid(2)`'s system-call number.
doc.markdown: `getpid(2)`'s system-call number.

doc.summary: Executes a raw Linux system call without arguments.
doc.markdown: Executes a raw Linux system call without arguments.
doc.returns: the kernel's raw result

items.name: Syscall6
items.signature: pub func Syscall6(number: uint64, arg0: uint64, arg1: uint64, arg2: uint64, arg3: uint64, arg4: uint64, arg5: uint64) -> int64

doc.summary: Executes a raw Linux system call with six arguments.
doc.markdown: Executes a raw Linux system call with six arguments.
doc.returns: the kernel's raw result

doc.summary: Widens a file descriptor to the register width a system call takes it in.
doc.markdown:
Widens a file descriptor to the register width a system call takes it in.
`fd` is read by value; the widened value is returned by copy. Sign extension is what matters: `-1` has to arrive
as all ones rather than as a small positive number, which is how `mmap` is told it has no backing descriptor.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: it sign-extended, so a negative one stays negative

doc.summary: A process identifier, as `getpid` and its relatives report one.
doc.markdown:
A process identifier, as `getpid` and its relatives report one.
Signed, because several calls overload the negative range to mean a process group.

doc.summary: A file descriptor, as the kernel numbers one.
doc.markdown:
A file descriptor, as the kernel numbers one.
Signed and small. A syscall taking one receives it sign-extended to a full register, which `SignExtendFd` does.

doc.summary: A byte offset within a file, which the 64-bit ABI makes 64 bits everywhere.
doc.markdown: A byte offset within a file, which the 64-bit ABI makes 64 bits everywhere.

doc.summary: A file's type and permission bits, as `open` and `stat` carry them.
doc.markdown: A file's type and permission bits, as `open` and `stat` carry them.

doc.summary: A user identifier.
doc.markdown: A user identifier.

doc.summary: A group identifier.
doc.markdown: A group identifier.

doc.summary: A duration or an instant, as seconds and nanoseconds.
doc.markdown:
A duration or an instant, as seconds and nanoseconds.
Both fields are 64 bits under the kernel's 64-bit ABI, whichever architecture. `nanoseconds` is in `[0, 999999999]`
for a value the kernel produced; a value the caller builds must normalize it, since a call given more than a
second's worth of nanoseconds reports `EINVAL` rather than carrying.
Passed by address to every call that reads or fills one.
